variable {p : ℕ} [hp : Fact p.Prime] {x y : ℤ_[p]}
informal_statement: For any non-zero element \( x \) in the \( p \)-adic integers \( \mathbb{Z}_p \), the norm of \( x \) is equal to \( p \) raised to the negative of the valuation of \( x \).
informal_proof: We begin by recalling the definition of the norm in the context of \( p \)-adic integers, which is directly related to the \( p \)-adic valuation of an element. By definition, the norm of an element \( x \) in \( \mathbb{Z}_p \) is given by \( \|x\| = p^{-v_p(x)} \), where \( v_p(x) \) denotes the \( p \)-adic valuation of \( x \). This relationship holds because the \( p \)-adic norm is constructed to measure the "size" of \( x \) inversely with respect to its \( p \)-adic valuation. Given that \( x \neq 0 \), this formula ensures that the norm is well-defined and positive, aligning with the properties of non-Archimedean norms in valuation theory. Thus, we arrive at the conclusion that \( \|x\| = p^{-v_p(x)} \) for any non-zero \( x \) in \( \mathbb{Z}_p \).

rag.content:
/-- `Padic.valuation` lifts the `p`-adic valuation on rationals to `ℚ_[p]`. -/
def valuation : ℚ_[p] → ℤ :=
  Quotient.lift (@PadicSeq.valuation p _) fun f g h ↦ by
    by_cases hf : f ≈ 0
    · have hg : g ≈ 0 := Setoid.trans (Setoid.symm h) hf
      simp [hf, hg, PadicSeq.valuation]
    · have hg : ¬g ≈ 0 := fun hg ↦ hf (Setoid.trans h hg)
      rw [PadicSeq.val_eq_iff_norm_eq hf hg]
      exact PadicSeq.norm_equiv h

protected theorem nonneg (q : ℚ) : 0 ≤ padicNorm p q :=

    split_ifs

variable {p : ℕ} [hp : Fact p.Prime] {x y : ℤ_[p]}
informal_statement: For any element \( x \) in the ring of integers localized at \( p \) (denoted \( \mathbb{Z}_{[p]} \)) and any natural number \( n \), the \( p \)-adic valuation of \( x^n \) is equal to \( n \) times the \( p \)-adic valuation of \( x \). In mathematical terms, \( \text{valuation}(x^n) = n \times \text{valuation}(x) \).
informal_proof:
Let's consider an arbitrary element \( x \) in the ring \( \mathbb{Z}_{[p]} \), which represents the integers localized at the prime \( p \), and let \( n \) be an arbitrary natural number. We aim to show that multiplying \( x \) by itself \( n \) times results in an element whose \( p \)-adic valuation is exactly \( n \) times the valuation of \( x \).

First, recall that the \( p \)-adic valuation, often denoted as \( v_p \), measures the highest power of \( p \) that divides a given integer. When working within the localized ring \( \mathbb{Z}_{[p]} \), this valuation extends naturally to elements of the ring.

To find the valuation of \( x^n \), we can utilize the property that multiplication in the localized ring interacts nicely with the \( p \)-adic valuation. Specifically, the valuation of a product of elements is the sum of their valuations. Applying this property \( n \) times as we multiply \( x \) by itself, we get:

\[
v_p(x^n) = v_p(x \times x \times \dots \times x) = v_p(x) + v_p(x) + \dots + v_p(x) = n \times v_p(x)
\]

This demonstrates that raising \( x \) to the power \( n \) simply multiplies its valuation by \( n \), as required.

informal_statement: For any two non-zero elements \( x \) and \( y \), the valuation of their product \( x \times y \) is equal to the sum of their individual valuations, \( \text{valuation}(x) + \text{valuation}(y) \).
informal_proof:
Assume that both \( x \) and \( y \) are non-zero elements. By the properties of valuations, specifically the behavior of the valuation function under multiplication for non-zero elements, we know that the valuation of the product \( x \times y \) is equal to the sum of the valuations of \( x \) and \( y \) individually. This follows directly from the lemma `Padic.valuation_mul`, which asserts that:

\[
\text{valuation}(x \times y) = \text{valuation}(x) + \text{valuation}(y)
\]

Thus, the statement is proven by applying this property under the given conditions that neither \( x \) nor \( y \) is zero.

open Padic Metric IsLocalRing

variable {p : ℕ} [hp : Fact p.Prime] {x y : ℤ_[p]}
informal_statement: For any element \( x \) in the p-adic field \( \mathbb{Q}_p \), the valuation of \( x \) is non-negative.
informal_proof:
First, consider the case where \( x \) is equal to \( 0 \). In this case, the valuation of \( 0 \) is directly known to be \( 0 \), which satisfies the non-negativity condition.

Next, suppose \( x \) is not equal to \( 0 \). Utilizing the properties of the p-adic norm and valuation, we know that the valuation of \( x \) is related to the p-adic norm of \( x \) in such a way that the norm of \( x \) is equal to the prime \( p \) raised to the negative of the valuation of \( x \). Specifically, \( |x|_p = p^{-v(x)} \), where \( v(x) \) denotes the valuation of \( x \).

Given that \( |x|_p \) is a non-negative real number and \( p \) is a prime number (greater than or equal to 2), it follows that \( p^{-v(x)} \) must also be non-negative. For the p-adic norm to be less than or equal to 1 (as per the properties of non-archimedean absolute values), the exponent \( -v(x) \) must be less than or equal to 0. This implies that \( v(x) \) must be greater than or equal to 0.

Since both scenarios—whether \( x \) is zero or not—are covered, we conclude that the valuation \( v(x) \) is always non-negative for any \( x \) in \( \mathbb{Q}_p \).

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
